articles.title: Social media bans are no cure-all, but governments may still find them necessary
articles.summary: Experts warn that social media bans may offer short-term safety but push young people to circumvent restrictions, making radicalization harder to detect

blocks.text: BALI, Indonesia – Restricting access to online platforms cannot address all the factors that contribute to the radicalization of young people, but governments have “valid” reasons for imposing bans, said I Gusti Agung Wesaka Puja, executive director of the ASEAN Institute for Peace and Reconciliation (ASEAN-IPR).
“There is no perfect solution, especially when we are encountering this new kind of threat, a new kind of non-traditional security issue,” Puja told Rappler in an interview on October 12.
Puja maintained that while governments may find it necessary to step in and implement social media bans to protect children from harmful content, these measures still require careful assessment.

“The government in this respect has the responsibility to consider the safety and well-being of young people because they are our future leaders, particularly as digital platforms continue to evolve and continue to provide a threat to them,” said Puja.
“However, whether restrictions on social media access will produce positive long-term outcomes, certainly this needs careful assessment,” he added.

Puja leads ASEAN’s think tank on peace and conflict. A recent study by ASEAN-IPR found that traditional security responses are insufficient to prevent violence as young people in Southeast Asia gain greater access to it.

The Philippine Senate has approved Senate Bill 2424 that restricts social media access of children under 16. The House of Representatives approved a similar measure or House Bill 11566. These legislative developments follow three school shootings in the country that occurred this year. (READ: Why Congress should think twice about banning under-18s from social media)
Indonesia also started implementing the ban early this year, and countries across the world are considering social media legislation, following the likes of Australia, the United Kingdom, and Brazil.

“Maybe putting some bans on the use of social media, it could be effective,” Bora Park, security and terrorism expert from Seoul-based Institute for National Security Strategy, told Rappler in a separate interview.

“But in the long term, it might also have a side effect,” Bora said, adding that young people may find ways to circumvent the regulations and create new slang, making it “much harder to detect which one is radicalized and how dangerous that individual would be.”
Skeptics of such measures cite their potential effects on young people’s access to information, education and opportunities, as well as their social interactions.
Implementation of the regulation remains uncertain, as it relies heavily on the cooperation of private technology companies.

Senator Risa Hontiveros, the sole Philippine lawmaker who voted against the bill on social media ban for kids, said the priority is how to effectively protect children. Hontiveros advocates for “tiered restrictions for adolescents.”

In her statement, Hontiveros said younger adolescents should have tighter restrictions. As kids age and mature, she proposed they be given “autonomy while protections remain against abuse, exploitation, and harmful content.”

“Taking it away from them all of a sudden without providing adequate ways for them to cope with its absence is not the answer to their needs and it is not the answer to our collective fears,” Hontiveros said.

articles.title: Barriers facing black and south Asian music events ‘cost London up to £141m a year’
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Investigation finds racial inequality in live music industry rife and many genres labelled ‘high risk’ despite lack of evidence

Black and south Asian music events in London face…

blocks.text: Black and south Asian music events in London face disproportionate cancellations, restrictions and licensing barriers compared with white events, according to a two-year investigation into racial inequality in the capital’s live music industry.

The Race Equality in Music Event Licensing (REMEL) report, led by Black Lives in Music, estimates that cancellations, displacement and events prevented from taking place cost London £127m to £141m annually, with projected losses exceeding £650m over five years.

The report found that genres including Afrobeats, drill and dancehall are routinely labelled “high risk” despite a lack of credible evidence, while indie, pop and rock events face comparatively little scrutiny.
Other events facing stringent restrictions included reggae gatherings aimed at older audiences, jazz nights and community events.
The research raised concerns over the use of unverified police intelligence, with promoters describing events being cancelled based on undisclosed information, online searches or unrelated incidents.
Charisse Beaumont, chief executive of Black Lives in Music, said that although the investigation focused on London, the problems it uncovered exist nationwide.
“As soon as we put the report out there, the call for our survey, people were upset that they couldn’t complete the survey because they were outside of London,” she said.
For Beaumont, the discrimination extended far beyond specific music genres. “It’s about race. And that’s what’s so deeply sad about it.”

blocks.caption: Charisse Beaumont of Black Lives in Music said that although the investigation focused on London, the problems were prevalent nationwide. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian

blocks.text: The two-year study was commissioned by the mayor’s office and included collaboration by the Greater London Authority (GLA), the Metropolitan Police Service, UK Music, LIVE, the Musicians’ Union and a wide network of promoters, artists, venue operators and community representatives.

The findings suggest that the legacy of the Metropolitan police’s controversial Form 696 persists. Introduced in 2005 as a risk assessment tool, it was scrapped in 2017 after criticism that it discriminated against black music events.

Hakeem Stevens, the report’s lead researcher, said police scrutiny had become harder to document. “Back in the day when emails were sent and faxes were sent, we had documented evidence. Now what’s happening is it’s whispers, it’s phone calls, it’s conversations, verbal conversations that can’t be recorded.”
He said black and Asian performers faced disproportionate scrutiny, adding: “You’ve got white artists that perform black music, and they don’t get given that level of scrutiny.”
Researchers found that promoters received little explanation for cancellations, faced substantial security costs and had limited opportunities to challenge decisions.
Stevens said the financial and reputational consequences could severely affect mental health.
Beaumont highlighted the case of the Colour Factory, a black-owned venue whose licence was suspended after an incident outside its premises that was reportedly unrelated to the venue.
She said the owner successfully challenged the decision but faced significant financial losses, including legal costs and staff redundancies.
“In the end, they won, but they didn’t get their money back,” she said.
The report also found that when incidents occur, many white-owned venues are supported back into business after incidents, while black-owned venues are forced to close for prolonged periods.
Kwame Otiende, a venue owner, promoter and Green councillor, said the additional scrutiny discouraged venues from hosting certain events.
“Venues will have known that they get a lot more grief from whatever relevant authorities they need to go through to get a temporary event notice,” he said.
Instead, he suggested, venues may opt for safer commercial choices: “I could just put your very sort of middle-of-the-road chart music … and I’ll still make the same amount of money.”

The report sets out 19 recommendations, including calls for more transparent, evidence-based licensing decisions, alongside an independent review, clearer evidence standards, better reporting of licensing outcomes and stronger accountability.

Beaumont said: “Success would be for me, the ability for any artist from any background, particularly Black and south Asian, to be able to perform and put on events at any venue without barriers, so they too can make money
“They’ve got an album out, they do a tour, they might be able to do a 1,000-capacity venue, but can they progress from 2,000 to 5,000 to 20,000 to stadium? That doesn’t happen for us.”

The Met police commander Neerav Patel said the force would carefully consider the reports finding. “Our focus will remain on making fair, evidence-based contributions to the licensing process which balance the interests of venues, promoters, artists and local communities while never compromising on our ultimate priority which is to keep Londoners safe” said Patel.

articles.title: How did Escudero rule so fast on prosecution’s surprise move?
articles.summary: As presiding officer of the impeachment court, Chiz Escudero anticipated and prepared for different scenarios in the course of the trial

blocks.text: Presiding officer Chiz Escudero addresses the court before the start of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on August 26, 2026.
Senate Social Media Unit
As presiding officer of the impeachment court, Chiz Escudero anticipated and prepared for different scenarios in the course of the trial

There were two surprises during Vice President Sara Duterte‘s impeachment trial on Tuesday, October 13: the bombshell motion of the prosecution to drop three of the four articles of impeachment, and the extensive ruling of presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero delivered less than an hour after the House prosecutors’ request.

So how did Escudero manage to make the ruling in such a short period of time? Senate impeachment court spokesperson Reginald Tongol said that Escudero, with his staff as well as Senate Clerk of Court Renato Bantug Jr., anticipated different scenarios and prepared rulings based on all legal possibilities.

“The presiding officer has prepared rulings for different scenarios but they were in skeletal in form. It still has to be drafted and finalized upon his delivery and formal manifestation in the court,” Tongol in a mix of English and Filipino during a press briefing after the trial on Tuesday, October 13.
Tongol cited the prosecution’s October 6 manifestation signaling its intent to withdraw Article III, which covers bribery, as an example of how Escudero anticipated possible developments.

“For example, the prosecution filed a manifestation to drop Article III on October 6, so with due diligence, the presiding officer prepared and anticipated whatever that is going to be thrown at him at the trial,” he said.

The prosecution ultimately went further, seeking to withdraw Article I, which covers the alleged misuse of confidential funds, and Article IV, which covers grave threats. The court granted the request, leaving only Article II, which concerns Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth.
Tongol said Escudero continued working on his ruling until shortly before delivering it, incorporating inputs from his fellow senator-judges.
“The presiding officer’s rulings considered the inputs of his fellow senator judges. That’s why up to the last minute, he was actually writing and editing his speech,” said Tongol.

This also explained why Escudero was cautious when Duterte’s defense counsel requested a copy of the ruling. Tongol said the presiding officer wanted the written version checked against the ruling delivered in court and reflected in the journal.

“That’s also the reason when the respondent’s counsel was asking for a copy of the ruling, he said he wanted to be careful and that his written speech should be compared to the delivered speech in the journal. The official ruling was the one delivered during the trial,” he added.
Escudero himself explained during the proceedings that the court had prepared for various possible scenarios to ensure it could address issues raised by either party.

The court sought to know “the same, if not more, than each party or both parties combined,” Escudero said, explaining that the preparation was intended to help the court address potential issues and consider different outcomes. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Investigators hunt French supermarket fridge hackers, no claim of responsibility
articles.summary: The absence of a claim of responsibility by hacktivists or a ransom demand by cybercriminals puzzles French investigators

blocks.text: REFRIGERATORS. View of empty refrigerators at the frozen food aisle inside an Intermarche supermarket in Paris the day after a cyberattack targeted refrigeration systems at French supermarket chains, causing food losses and fires at several stores, France, October 13, 2026.
Lucien Libert/Reuters
The absence of a claim of responsibility by hacktivists or a ransom demand by cybercriminals puzzles French investigators

items: French investigators are searching for hackers who compromised cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets, with no group claiming responsibility for the cyberattack.
The breach was linked to outdated software from Danfoss, which affected the refrigeration systems of several supermarket chains, leading to significant food waste.
Cybersecurity experts highlighted the importance of basic cyber hygiene, noting that many vulnerable systems remain accessible online, posing ongoing risks.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

PARIS, France – French investigators on Tuesday, October 13, were hunting the hackers who seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets in a cyberattack that underlined the vulnerabilities of connected systems, with no group publicly claiming responsibility.

The investigation comes as Dutch supermarket company Ahold Delhaize grapples with a separate cybersecurity incident that disrupted online services, although Dutch authorities said they saw no connection between the two events.

The absence of a claim of responsibility by hacktivists or a ransom demand by cybercriminals has puzzled French investigators, according to a source with knowledge of the probe. Typically, such groups tend to quickly seek to monetize their hacks or claim credit for them for political ends.

The cyberattack, which manually overrode the temperatures at fridges in supermarket groups including Carrefour, Monoprix, Intermarche, and Cooperative U, appears to have been easy to pull off, three cyber experts told Reuters.

Staff at some Paris supermarkets threw boxes full of perished meat and frozen goods into giant trash containers on Tuesday. At least 350 supermarkets — a small fraction of the total number in France — were caught up in the strike.
France’s cybersecurity agency has said the breach affected fridges that relied on software by Danish firm Danfoss, as well as Copeland and Dixell software.

Danfoss said on Monday that many of the affected units had “reached end of life and no longer receive software or security updates” or were “running outdated firmware.” It said it had “advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions”.
The company declined further comment on Tuesday.
Copeland, which owns Dixell, acknowledged the “vulnerability.”
“We are currently working with impacted customers to mitigate the risk,” the company said, adding that it would strengthen cybersecurity.
In Danfoss’ case, the serious vulnerabilities present in older versions of its firmware have been known for months.

On August 9, cybersecurity firm Claroty detailed weaknesses — since patched — in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A controller that could have allowed intruders to bypass authentication and run code on compromised devices.

Although the precise mechanism by which attackers compromised the refrigerators has not been publicly disclosed, cybersecurity experts said all signs pointed to a basic stunt enabled both by the failure to adopt Danfoss’ updates and by exposing device interfaces to the internet.
“This is about basic cyber hygiene,” said Ken Munro, a partner at the British cybersecurity firm Pen Test Partners. “Get it wrong and you get a smelly mess of defrosted food.”
He said the well-known vulnerabilities meant the attackers were essentially pushing at an open door, something that meant the hack could easily be “kids messing around”.

“If this was a nation state, why affect only a subset of French fridges? There are plenty of other nations with fridges on the internet,” he said. “No ransom or demand suggests a lack of appreciation of the potential commercial losses that the fridge owners may experience.”
Plenty of fridges remain reachable via the internet. Using the internet scanning service Shodan, Reuters found at least 4,500 Danfoss interfaces still viewable on Tuesday.

Reuters could not independently establish how many of them were running vulnerable software, but French internet scanning company Onyphe said only a small minority of the devices appeared to be running the latest version of the software.
Outdated and vulnerable versions were “still widely represented among publicly accessible interfaces”, Onyphe said.
Separately, Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize said on Tuesday it had begun “starting a controlled re-launch of certain systems” following a cybersecurity issue that began on Sunday evening.
The Dutch cybersecurity watchdog NCSC said it did not believe the incident was linked to the French supermarket hack.

Ahold operates the Albert Heijn chain in the Netherlands and several major US chains including Stop & Shop and Giant Food. Websites for stores in both countries remained offline late Tuesday afternoon, with online ordering and delivery services unavailable. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 51% of Filipinos want Sara Duterte to testify at her impeachment trial -- Pulse Asia
articles.summary: A slim majority of Filipino adults, or 51%, believe Vice President Sara Duterte should testify in person before the Senate impeachment court, according to a Pulse Asia survey.

blocks.text: Published October 14, 2026 12:50pm
A slim majority of Filipino adults, or 51%, believe Vice President Sara Duterte should testify in person before the Senate impeachment court, according to a Pulse Asia survey.
The 2026 Nationwide Survey on the Impeachment Case and Trial of the Vice-President showed that the sentiment was shared by majorities of respondents in Metro Manila (66%) and the rest of Luzon (61%).
The same view was expressed by 56% of respondents in socioeconomic Class ABC (upper- and middle-income households) and 53% in Class D (lower-income households).
Meanwhile, 34% of Filipino adults said Duterte should not personally appear before the impeachment court, 14% were undecided, and 1% declined to express an opinion.
Opposition to Duterte's personal appearance was highest in Mindanao, where 61% of respondents said she should not testify.
Nearly half of respondents in Class E (48%), representing the lowest-income households, shared this view.
Knowledge of impeachment case
The survey also found that 53% of Filipino adults admitted knowing little about the impeachment case against Duterte.
This included 48% of respondents in Metro Manila, 55% in the rest of Luzon, 51% in the Visayas, and 52% in Mindanao.
In Class ABC, a slight majority (52%) said they had sufficient knowledge of the case. However, majorities in Class D (54%) and Class E (60%) admitted knowing little about it.
Despite their limited knowledge, 55% of Filipino adults expressed interest in Duterte's impeachment trial.
Another 20% said they were not interested, while 25% were undecided.
The survey also identified the internet (64%) and television (59%) as the leading sources of information about the impeachment proceedings.
Radio was cited by 15% of respondents, while fewer than 1% relied on newspapers.
Meanwhile, 9% of Filipino adults said they were not following the impeachment trial.
Unexplained wealth allegations
The survey also showed that 71% of Filipino adults were aware of the allegations concerning Duterte's supposed unexplained wealth.
However, 39% of respondents said they could not determine whether the allegations were true or false.
"Several changes in awareness levels and public opinion regarding the truthfulness of these allegations occur between July 2026 and September 2026," Pulse Asia said.
According to the polling firm, nationwide awareness of the allegations declined by 10 percentage points between July and September 2026.
The decline was also recorded in Metro Manila (13 percentage points), the rest of Luzon (14 percentage points), Mindanao (9 percentage points), and Class D (11 percentage points).
Methodology
The Pulse Asia survey was conducted from September 17 to 24, 2026, through face-to-face interviews with 2,400 Filipino adults.
It had a margin of error of ±2 percentage points at the 95% confidence level.
Subnational estimates for Metro Manila, the rest of Luzon, the Visayas, and Mindanao each had a margin of error of ±4 percentage points at the same confidence level.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Agri chief revokes import permit of seized imported Vietnamese rice
articles.summary: Agri chief revokes import permit of seized imported Vietnamese rice

blocks.text: Published October 14, 2026 12:47pm

Department of Agriculture Secretary Francis Tiu Laurel Jr. said on Wednesday that it was him who ordered the cancellation of the import permit for rice from aboard MV Tay Son after receiving a “derogatory” information about the shipment.

“The records will show otherwise. It was the DA, through my office, that stopped the shipment by ordering the Bureau of Plant Industry (BPI) to cancel its sanitary and phytosanitary import clearance, even though the vessel was already on its way to the Philippines,” Tiu Laurel said.
“Critics of the DA are painting a false picture of this incident, suggesting malice and corruption through insinuations that border on libel,” he added.

The shipment was supposedly bound for Davao Occidental, but the Bureau of Customs and the Philippine Navy reportedly intercepted the vessel. This was after the DA’s BPI revoked the PPI’s sanitary and phytosanitary import clearances and notified the Port of Davao.

“The DA chief said the import permit was canceled at the request of Planters Product Inc. (PPI), which was importing 25-percent broken rice but was informed that the shipment contained 5-percent broken rice,” the department’s statement read.
“He added that PPI also notified him that the importation contract had already expired, as the delivery was originally scheduled for July, a period when rice supply is typically tight.”
The DA also said the vessel carrying the imported rice arrived at the Port of Davao last September 14 without a valid SPIC, and the captain refused BPI’s inspection.
On September 17, the ship departed Davao without clearance.
The Philippine Navy later intercepted the vessel off Sarangani and brought it to the Port of General Santos City, where the captain continued to resist inspection by the BPI.
Tiu Laurel said the BPI had recommended returning the rice to its country of origin and was awaiting action by the BOC.

“The BOC may instead seize the shipment and impose penalties, depending on its findings and the applicable rules. In either case, the vessel remains subject to penalties arising from the incident,” the DA said. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Judge extends White House access to banned media outlets CNN, MS Now and Politico
articles.summary:
District court judge Timothy Kelly was ruling after the Trump administration blocked access to the three outlets in September

A federal judge ordered the White House on Tuesday to continue…

blocks.text: A federal judge ordered the White House on Tuesday to continue allowing journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico to access the building as the media coalition’s lawsuit against the Trump administration plays out.

Timothy Kelly, a district court judge, had on 24 September granted a 14-day reprieve for the news organizations, which six days earlier had been banned by the president in an extraordinary move from entering the White House grounds “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS”.

“Defendants (except for President Trump) and their agents, representatives, and all persons or entities acting in concert with them, shall not execute, implement, or enforce the September 18, 2026, decision to revoke the White House ‘hard pass’ press credentials held by employees of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO, thereby maintaining the status quo since the Court’s entry of a temporary restraining order on September 24, 2026,” the judge wrote in granting a preliminary injunction requested by the plaintiffs.

The organizations filed a lawsuit on 21 September seeking to overturn the ban as a violation of their rights under the US constitution. But that temporary restraining order expired on Tuesday, bringing the media companies into court late last week to ask for a preliminary injunction that would lift the ban during the duration of the lawsuit, which could take months.

During arguments at the E Barrett Prettyman Federal Courthouse in Washington, Kelly seemed inclined to lift the ban indefinitely, telling a lawyer for the federal government that his side had “a notice problem” that was “probably the biggest hurdle” they had to overcome.

The Trump White House gave no advance notice to the media companies affected to say that they were at risk of losing their press badges, which the news organizations have said are essential to their ability to cover the administration. While the White House sent letters to the media companies informing them of the ban, they did so post-hoc, after building access had already been cut off, in violation of binding court precedent.

In his ruling on Tuesday, Judge Kelly wrote that the plaintiffs “are likely to succeed not only on their due process claim, but also on their two First Amendment claims”. While access to the White House is not guaranteed, court precedent dictates that once it is provided to journalists, it cannot be taken away for editorial or viewpoint-based reasons.

During arguments for a preliminary injunction on 8 October, media lawyer Theodore J Boutrous told the judge that Trump had offered a “confession” – in a Time magazine interview last week – that he was banning the media companies explicitly because of the content of their reporting, not because of any other considerations, such as national security.
“The case has gotten stronger for the plaintiffs thanks to President Trump,” Boutrous told the judge.

The judge seemed to agree. “President Trump’s own comments suggest that he intended the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes to alter their reporting on him, bolstering the case that his action here is sufficient to deter a reporter of ordinary firmness from reporting in the same way she had before,” he wrote.

Although the White House has largely adhered to the judge’s prior ruling restoring access on a temporary basis, journalists for CNN and Politico have on occasion been prevented from performing “pool duty” – covering the daily activities of the president – because the administration has interpreted the judge’s temporary restraining order to solely require access to the White House complex, not smaller spaces like Air Force One or the Oval Office.
The judge required the media plaintiffs to post a bond of $1.

In a statement, Boutrous said of the judge’s ruling: “When the President issued his ‘ban on the free press,’ he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment. Since then, the President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn’t like and to try to force journalists to cover him in ways he prefers.”
The court, he added, “was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this ‘unconstitutional ban on the free press’ for the foreseeable future”.

articles.title: Withdrawal of impeach charges denied Sara Duterte a chance to clear her name — spox
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte was deprived of the opportunity to refute the allegations against her in the Senate impeachment court after prosecutors withdrew three of the four articles of impeachment,…

blocks.text: Headlines
October 14, 2026 | 12:30pm
Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Senate in Pasay City on July 7, 2026 to meet with members of her defense team ahead of the continuation of her impeachment trial.
The Philippine STAR / Ryan Baldemor

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte was deprived of the opportunity to refute the allegations against her in the Senate impeachment court after prosecutors withdrew three of the four articles of impeachment, her spokesperson said.

In a statement posted on Facebook on Wednesday, October 14, Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr. described the withdrawal as an injustice, arguing that it prevented the vice president from presenting evidence in her defense and obtaining an acquittal on the charges.
“The withdrawal is an admission that the allegations lacked basis from the very beginning,” Panelo said.

“Yet, it is also an injustice and a denial of due process because it deprives the Vice President of the opportunity to confront these charges and present countervailing evidence in the proper forum, which is the Senate Impeachment Court,” he added.
Panelo said Duterte was also deprived of the opportunity to obtain an acquittal based on the evidence and the law.
“More than that, it deprived her of the vindication of the acquittal she deserves if the Court ruled only on the basis of evidence and law,” he said.
The spokesperson also questioned the public funds spent on the withdrawn charges, estimating that the total cost of the proceedings could exceed P1 billion.

He claimed the Senate spent around P500 million in operating costs on the alleged misuse of confidential funds and grave threats charges alone, excluding lawmakers’ salaries and other expenses. He did not provide a detailed breakdown to support his estimate.
Panelo further questioned whether political considerations ahead of the 2028 elections influenced the prosecution’s decision to withdraw the articles.

The House prosecution panel, meanwhile, said it would focus on Article II, which concerns Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth, failure to fully declare her assets and failure to divest from business interests.
Lead prosecutor Rep. Jinky Luistro described the decision to pursue only one article as the “most judicious course,” citing the need to narrow the case and expedite the proceedings.

The court ruled that Articles I and IV were withdrawn with prejudice, meaning they cannot be revived against Duterte in an impeachment trial during her current term. Article III, which concerns bribery, was withdrawn without prejudice because prosecutors had not yet presented evidence on it.
The court also lifted restrictions on public discussion of the withdrawn articles, allowing both the prosecution and the defense to address the allegations outside the trial.
Duterte’s defense team objected to the ruling, arguing that the vice president would no longer be able to present evidence in court to rebut the withdrawn charges.
The impeachment court has set November 9 as the start of Duterte’s presentation of evidence on the remaining article.

articles.title: $20m public liability insurance to rally in a park: how council red tape hinders the right to protest
articles.summary:
Public gatherings stymied by bureaucracy, Australian Democracy Network and Deakin University researchers find

  • Get our

blocks.text: Council red tape is stymieing the right to protest, a report has said, after a regional New South Wales council told a protest organiser they needed a $20m public liability insurance policy to hold a rally in a park.

A report released on Wednesday, co-authored by Australian Democracy Network (ADN) and Deakin University’s Centre for Law as Protection, raised concerns about incidents in which councils have required protest organisers to obtain insurance when rallies are held on council land.
It also expressed concern about the power some regional and urban councils have to issue financial penalties if public gatherings are held without a council permit.

In July, Mariella Gussoni notified Bathurst regional council she was holding a protest in a local park against the culling of brumbies in Kosciuszko national park. In her email to the council, seen by Guardian Australia, she said the protest would be part of nationwide rallies on a set day in August. The protest would include speakers and music, and she wasn’t sure if five or 50 people would attend, she wrote.

The council responded by letter, seen by Guardian Australia, saying it would permit her to hold her planned protest on the condition she take out a $20m public liability insurance policy, noting the council would not be liable for any loss or injury.

Nervous about what that could mean, and how much it would cost, the 61-year-old decided to hold the protest, which was attended by an estimated 120 people, next to the park. She notified police of her intention to hold the rally on the footpath – which is not council land – and said it went ahead without any issues.
“It scared me that I would be liable,” she said. “I had just let the council know as a courtesy.”
A spokesperson for Bathurst council said: “Council engaged with the event organisers at the time and won’t be providing any further comment on the matter.”

Report co-author and ADN protest rights campaigner, Anastasia Radievska, said council red tape such as insurance requirements could have a chilling effect on people speaking up about what’s happening in their local neighbourhoods.
“Often, community groups might spring up in relation to a specific local issue,” she said. “The more councils do this, the more other councils think that this is the way to interact with protest.”

The report said that across most Australian jurisdictions, “protest is unlawful or unprotected” without “permission from police, councils or place managers” and called for existing permit systems to be considered a process of notification rather than authorisation. It also recommended there be no insurance requirements.

NSW carries a $2,200 fine if a public gathering is held on council land without a permit, the report noted. This is a default requirement under the Local Government Act, but some councils have their own policies which deviate from the act. The city of Sydney has passed a number of motions affirming the right to protest on council land.

This requirement exists in addition to the police’s form 1 process, in which protesters can notify police of an intention to protest and gain immunity from being charged for offences such as obstructing a road in a designated area.
Tim Roberts, the president of the Council for Civil Liberties, said council demands for insurance or permits were “unhelpful” and a “reactionary approach”.
“It’s a blatant contravention of the right to protest,” Roberts said, referring to the implied right to freedom of political communication in the Australian constitution.
after newsletter promotion

He agreed that protest organisers should only be required to give notice and not seek authorisation. He equated the council requiring insurance with calls for a user-pays system for the policing of protests.

Last week, a community group opposing a proposed $2.9bn datacentre on Sydney’s Cooks River was told by Bayside council it needed public liability insurance to hold a rally at Cahill Park in Wolli Creek.

The council also told the organisers it required an event application because their event included food, a film, and amplified sound. One of the organisers for Stop the Cooks River AI Project (SCRAP), Caitlin Boyce, said the council said it would need eight weeks to assess the application.

After receiving pro bono legal advice, the group decided to take their chances and go ahead with the protest without making an event application to the council. Boyce said she hasn’t heard from the council since going ahead with the rally.

A spokesperson for the Bayside council said it was not opposed to the public gathering, but the planned activities – which it said included a barbecue and smoking ceremony – “constitute an organised event and are subject to Council’s event approval requirements”.
Local Government NSW and the Office of Local Government were approached for comment.

articles.title: Russia arrests Japanese journalist on alleged espionage
articles.summary: The Hokkaido Shimbun journalist is accused of collecting information on Moscow's defence capabilities for Tokyo.

blocks.text: Russian authorities have charged a Japanese journalist for espionage, accusing him of gathering information related to Moscow's defence capabilities for Tokyo.
The journalist, identified as Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun, was detained in Russia's far eastern region of Sakhalin, a day before he was due to leave the country.
The arrest comes as tensions worsen between the two nations after Russian leader Vladimir Putin visited the disputed Kuril Islands, claimed by both countries, in August.
Japan has not commented at length on the arrest. On Tuesday, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said authorities are "verifying the facts" and will "respond appropriately" thereafter.

Russian authorities allege that Imai had "acted on the instructions of [Japan's] national intelligence service" to gather information about people involved in a special military operation on the Kuril Islands, state news agency TASS reported.

The Kuril islands sit between Hokkaido in northern Japan and Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula. The archipelago is administered by Russia, but four of the southernmost islands are claimed by Japan, which calls them the Northern Territories.
Imai has been taken to Moscow and will be remanded until 12 December, before the trial begins, according to Interfax, another Russian news agency.
Those convicted of espionage in Russia can be jailed up to 20 years in prison.

"Tokyo's attempts to use its correspondents in Russia, who hold foreign journalist status, to gather information aimed at undermining our country's security are regrettable," Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said in a statement on Tuesday.
"We cannot help but point out that today's incident is not an isolated one," she noted, but did not name other journalists or media outlets that are allegedly involved in similar activity.
Imai's published work has covered Russia's relations with North Korea and life in Sakhalin.
Hokkaido Shimbun ran a report on the arrest without naming the reporter, but did not comment further on the incident.
Russia and Japan have been locked in a dispute over the Kurils for decades, and it is the main reason Moscow and Tokyo did not sign a peace treaty after World War Two.

Takaichi slammed Putin's visit in August – his first-ever to the islands – saying it "wounded the feelings of the Japanese people" and is "incompatible with Japan's consistent position on the Northern Territories".
Moscow dismissed her criticism as "politically inappropriate" and "legally unfounded".

Over the years, attempts to resolve the territorial dispute have made little progress. Bilateral ties have also remained frosty, with Japan imposing sanctions against Russia for its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Last week, Moscow again angered Tokyo for requesting the extradition of the president of the International Criminal Court (ICC), who is Japanese.
The president Tomoko Akane, along with other ICC officials, has been placed on Russia's wanted list since 2023 after the court issued an arrest warrant for Putin over war crimes in Ukraine.
In 2023, Russia detained The Wall Street Journal's Evan Gershkovich on espionage charges and later sentenced him to 16 years in prison.
Gershkovich, a US citizen, was in 2024 released in a prisoner swap, the largest exchange since the Cold War took place.

In 2019, Moscow detained an unnamed Japanese journalist from Kyodo News on suspicion of attempting to obtain military secrets. The journalist, who was picked up in Vladivostok, was ordered to leave the country within 72 hours.

articles.title: Iranian woman handed death sentence for ‘blasphemy’ in social media post
articles.summary:
Rights groups warn of Tehran regime’s increasing use of executions to suppress dissent, with at least 600 this year

Human rights groups have raised the alarm over the growing number of death…

blocks.text: Human rights groups have raised the alarm over the growing number of death sentences and executions in Iran, after reports that a 23-year-old woman, Najmeh Amini, has been sentenced to death for blasphemy over a social-media post.

Amini, an accounting student, is being held in Vakilabad prison in the north-east city of Mashhad. She has been sentenced to more than 12 years in prison and death in separate cases heard by a revolutionary and a criminal court.
A source close to Amini’s family told the US-based Human Rights Activists in Iran (HRAI) that Amini was sentenced to death on charges of “sab ol-nabi” (insulting the prophet).
In the second case, Amini was sentenced to 12 years, six months and one day on charges including acting against national security and spreading propaganda against the regime.

Amini was arrested by security forces during January’s nationwide protests, which were suppressed with a deadly crackdown. Thousands were reported killed, while the HRAI news agency, Hrana, said more than 50,000 people were arrested.
In an audio recording released from the prison last month, Amini appealed for international intervention, calling on the UN, lawyers and rights groups to investigate her case.
“I do not want to make a hero out of myself today. I only want one thing: be my voice,” she said.

“I am an innocent young girl with so many hopes and dreams,” Amini said. “I have parents who are waiting for me. A family that every night, with the fear of losing me, turns their night into morning.”

Rights groups warn that the Iranian authorities are increasingly using capital punishment to instil fear and suppress dissent. According to the Oslo-based Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO), more than 600 executions have already been carried out this year.

blocks.caption: Iranians block a Tehran street during nationwide protests in January, which were sparked by the weak economy but became political and anti-regime.  Photograph: Mahsa/Middle East Images/AFP

blocks.text: Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam, director of IHRNGO, said Amini’s case should be seen as a serious warning.

“Sentencing a young woman to death for what she posted on social media risks normalising the use of the death penalty against peaceful expression and pushing the boundaries of the death penalty even further,” he said.

Amiry-Moghaddam added that the Iranian authorities were testing the international community’s “tolerance” towards capital punishment. “If the international community does not respond firmly now, cases like this could become far more common,” he said.

Under article 262 of Iran’s Islamic penal code, insulting the prophet Muhammad or revered Shia figures is punishable by death. However, article 263 provides exemptions for statements made while intoxicated or without deliberate intent, although offenders may still face up to 74 lashes in certain circumstances.

According to the Iranian newspaper Khorasan, which confirmed the judicial proceedings, Amini told the court she had posted the remarks while hallucinating after taking psychedelic mushrooms with friends and her defence argued it was a “slip of the tongue”.
The presiding judge rejected her defence, reportedly asking: “Why, in that same hallucinatory state, did you not insult other individuals or opponents of the regime, such as America and Israel?”
Amini’s death sentence is not final and remains subject to appeal before Iran’s supreme court.
The student’s sentencing comes at a time when Iranian lawmakers are seeking to criminalise contact with all foreign media, including posts on social media deemed to be financed by another country.
Elnaz*, 24, who took part in the protests in Tehran in January and was arrested over social-media posts at the height of the war in March, said she lived in constant fear of surveillance.

“I was arrested even though my social-media account was private. So it’s not just the regime’s cyber-police we have to worry about. There’s also this constant mistrust, this feeling that someone is watching me all the time, even when I’m alone in my room.
“I’m scared to post anything on social media … but after everything they’ve put us through, do we really have anything left to lose? They can kill us even if we don’t post anything on social media.”

Although executions in Iran have surged in recent years, reaching their highest level in three decades, death sentences for blasphemy remain relatively rare. The last documented case was on 8 May 2023, when Yousef Mehrad and Sadrollah Fazeli-Zare were executed after being convicted of blasphemy-related offences tied to social-media activity.
* Name has been changed to protect her identity

articles.title: Ukraine is littered with landmines on a scale last seen in Vietnam. How can they be removed?
articles.summary:
Faced with deadlier threats, demining groups are coming up with new ways of working using drones and AI

Crouched over on her hands and knees in a field of weeds, Olena Kabanova is digging…
articles.byline: Amy Hawkins in Kharkiv region. Photographs by Julia Kochetova

blocks.text: Crouched over on her hands and knees in a field of weeds, Olena Kabanova is digging into the ground. With a shovel and a steady hand, the 58-year-old digs out a neat square around the spot where a mine detector has sensed a suspicious object.

Four years ago, this field in eastern Ukraine was occupied by Russian soldiers. Now back under Ukrainian control, it is littered with landmines. Civilians such as Kabanova are trying to make the land usable again.

Landmines are a scourge of conflict zones. Littered across contested territory, they leave land unusable for years after a war has ended. Removing them is an expensive and dangerous job. And the use of long-range drones in Ukraine, which is often described as the most mine-contaminated country in the world, is increasing the scale of the problem.

blocks.caption: Different types of ammunition presented at the Halo Trust office in Kharkiv. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian

blocks.text: “What we’re now seeing is the massive increase in the use of drone-delivered munitions,” says Paul Heslop, the programme manager for mine action at the United Nations Development Programme in Ukraine. “What already was a very high-intensity battle area is now potentially, through the use of drones on both sides, becoming a much wider area of contamination and a scale that we haven’t seen since the Americans were dropping cluster munitions on the Ho Chi Minh trail.”

blocks.caption: Olena Kabanova, a deminer with the Halo Trust, working at the site in the Kharkiv region. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian

blocks.text: The task of clearing landmines from Ukraine is replete with challenges. Drone and missile attacks make working outdoors unsafe; humanitarian workers are sometimes directly targeted. And newer, deadlier threats are also appearing. They include the POM-3, a small cylindrical mine used by Russian forces that could be mistaken for an abandoned vacuum flask. It is detonated by the vibrations of approaching footsteps.

POM-3 mines mean there are “specific villages that we just completely avoid”, says Anda Riza, a unit commander of the Halo Trust, the largest international humanitarian demining organisation in Ukraine, which employs Kabanova in the field in Kharkiv. The types of landmines are “constantly developing and evolving”, says Valeriia Shumska, Riza’s colleague.

blocks.caption: Valeriia Shumska, an operations support manager with the Halo Trust, at the site in the Kharkiv region. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian

blocks.text: But the technological innovation that is emerging from the conflict is also helping deminers to come up with new ways of working, which they hope are quicker and safer than the traditional hands-and-knees approach. The advances are being supported by the $1.5bn funding that has poured into Ukraine’s demining sector since the start of the full-scale invasion.

Take Kabanova’s job. Digging out a patch of land could take up to 45 minutes. But a new machine can do it in five. Called the DMR-7, it is a small, tank-like vehicle fitted with a hosepipe that shoots out jet flows of compressed air.

The tank is operated by a human using a remote controller who stands at a safe distance away. The operator manoeuvres the tank into place and then, with a loud mechanical whirring and plumes of dirt billowing skywards, the DMR-7 uses the force of compressed air to blast away a small patch of soil. It is a bulky, expensive alternative to a shovel, but it’s one that deminers hope can make one of the most dangerous parts of the demining process quicker and safer.

blocks.caption: Using a remote control, an operator moves a grenade found at the demining site. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian

blocks.text: The DMR-7 is just one of a host of new pieces of kit that the Halo Trust is experimenting with in Ukraine. Other technologies include AI-powered image analysis, ground-penetrating radar and devices that can detect explosive material, not just metal.

Just as drones have transformed the battlefield, they have also created new opportunities for humanitarians. Before 2022, much of Halo’s surveillance work – looking for signs of explosives – was done with binoculars and maps. Now it is done with drones, and satellite imagery, which can be analysed with the help of AI.

But war has also led to innovations in anti-drone technology. Drone jamming systems, used by both Russian and Ukrainian forces, can interfere with humanitarian work. Halo has lost several drones to jamming and spoofing attacks.
And the advances in new technology are not spread equally between providers.

In a field adjacent to one that Kabanova is working in, staff from the state emergency services are also clearing mines. Under the glare of the late summer sun, Mykyta Shulzhenko, the head of the mechanised demining unit, says his colleagues have started using drones for surveillance. But they are not yet able to use AI to analyse the drone-captured imagery. “I really hope this kind of technology will be implemented soon in our work,” he says.

blocks.caption: Mykyta Shulzhenko, the head of the mechanised demining unit of the state emergency service of Ukraine, at a demining site in the Kharkiv region. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian

blocks.text: The Halo Trust alone spent nearly £50m in Ukraine in the year to 31 March 2025, dwarfing the state’s annual budget of £28.6m for a programme to clear agricultural land of mines and unexploded ordnance. And there are dozens of other demining organisations with overlapping responsibilities and approaches. Responsibility for the sector is split across multiple government agencies. Attempts to reform the country’s mine action law to bring it in line with international standards have faltered.

Ihor Bezkaravainyi, a deputy economy minister who leads the country’s work on demining, wants to streamline the policymaking process to create one cabinet-level office to oversee the whole sector. But progress has been slow. Asked why, he offers a weary shrug: “Because, people.”

blocks.caption: Ihor Bezkaravainyi, a deputy economy minister, leads work on demining in Ukraine.  Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian

blocks.text: “When we’re talking about a new law, it will mean that some government bodies will lose responsibility, and, they think, power,” Bezkaravainyi says.
One person who has worked in Ukraine’s demining sector puts it more bluntly: “The biggest barrier to demining Ukraine is the government of Ukraine.”
Bezkaravainyi says: “When we’re talking about an ordinary situation with mine action … the conflict has ended, and the government does not exist … in Ukraine, it’s the opposite situation.”

That leads to a host of regulatory and bureaucratic barriers. For example, deminers are often prevented from using vehicles that are driven directly by a person, with health and safety standards requiring that the vehicles are operated remotely. Riza says: “We know for a fact that doing it remotely is much slower than having a person in the cab. That continues to be our biggest challenge.”

blocks.caption: A deminer operating remotely behind a protective shield. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian

blocks.text: Heslop argues that the Ukrainian authorities are overly broad in their categorisation of land as being contaminated by mines, an approach that risks wasting time and money on clearing land that wasn’t dangerous in the first place. “Just because it was occupied by the Russians doesn’t necessarily mean it was contaminated,” he says. “Land is only contaminated if it’s got fucking explosives in it.”

But deminers across the sector agree that technological advances will accelerate their ability to release Ukraine’s richly fertile land for civilian use at a much faster rate than has been possible in the past.
“This is the cutting edge of technology,” says Heslop. “This is where the humanitarian mine action sector is going through the biggest pivot in the last 30 years.”
Additional research by Illia Dyadik and Artem Mazhulin

blocks.text: A US federal judge has extended the order to allow three US media outlets to report from the White House, despite the Trump administration trying to ban them.
The three outlets, CNN, MS NOW and Politico, filed a lawsuit against the decision due to constitutional free speech and due process claims.
In September, District Judge Timothy Kelly issued an order to temporarily restore the journalists' access to the White House.

On Tuesday, Judge Kelly rulled that President Donald Trump likely broke the law by trying to ban them. He then issued a preliminary injunction to extend this previous order for the duration of the case.
